I have another suggestion which I should like to make to hon. members, and I hope they will consider it favourably. I am not putting it forward at the moment or until I learn at first-hand the sense of the house. I believe with members generally that much more of the work of parliament could and 100-3J
should be done by committees, and that we would save much general discussion if that were more largely adopted as a method of procedure. We have been accustomed to sitting just half a day on Wednesdays. I believe that we would make more progress during the session if one day in the week were reserved entirely for the work of committees. Members of parliament complain that they cannot serve on committees and watch proceedings in the house at the same time. I am sure it would be a convenience to members generally if there were one day which they could devote entirely to the work of the committees.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Now that the right hon. gentleman has brought up this matter, has he given any thought to an alternative scheme under which the time of parliament could be utilized to better effect with a different division of work as between the committees and the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, I have given a good deal of thought to it. One aspect to which necessarily I have had to give the most thought is how the government itself can adequately cope with the questions that come before it from day to day as the issues-become larger and more serious, with the war reaching the stage which it has reached at the present time. As horn, members know, the cabinet is obliged to meet every day. In addition there is the war committee of the cabinet which is concerned immediately with policy in respect to all the important matters that come up in connection with the war. Ministers of the crown cannot, I believe, give the time that is,needed for the careful consideration of the war and other measures that come before this parliament during a war session at. the stage the war has now reached without having some day which they can regard more1 or less as their own for purposes of careful consideration of the different measures. I believe that if, after all committees are appointed, it were generally understood that Wednesdays would be devoted to the work of committees, we would be serving alike the interests of parliament and the interests of the nation.

speechtext:
I am suggesting that for consideration. But that would not mean for a minute that the members will not be fully occupied. I think the public would understand that there will be plenty of work for all to do. It will result, I believe, in a.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
fuller attendance in the house when we are dealing with important matters, and in much less discussion and help to avoid undue prolongation of the sessions.
I shall leave it to my colleagues in the government to take up other matters which have been referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Graydon).
There is, however, one question which I shall necessarily have to deal with because it has become an issue in the country at the present time. The leader of the opposition stated that he noticed that the speech from the throne had to do with international organization-but that it made no special reference to what I presume he meant were the constitutional relations within the empire. My hon. friend himself made no statement on that important question. May I say to him that I think the country will wish to know where the Progressive Conservative party stands on the question raised of the relations of the different parts of the empire, as it will wish to know where the government stands and where the other parties represented in this house also stand.
May I say- that I hope the debate on the address will not be made the occasion for the discussion at length of matters that pertain to external affairs. There is an appropriate time for different subjects to be discussed. I would myself have preferred to say nothing whatever to-day on the matter to which I have just referred if it were not that statements have been made from sources I cannot ignore, and the country is expecting that I should make a statement of the government's position. But there will be during the course of the session an opportunity, when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs are before us, to discuss fully all matters of foreign policy, and I would hope that that would be the time at which such further discussion as may be necessary on some at least of these matters would take place.
I notice in a dispatch from Britain that on January 27 the question was raised in the House of Commons at Westminster as to whether the government did not think a debate on empire affairs at this stage was necessary in view of certain views recently expressed on empire relationship. The acting leader of the house, the deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Attlee, said that he thought such a discussion would not at that stage serve a useful purpose, and that other opportunities might come. I mention this simply that hon. members will see I am not taking a different view' in suggesting another time
[Mr. Mackenzie Kinir.l
for the discussion of foreign affairs than in the debate on the address. I am not seeking to rule out such a discussion, but I am seeking indirectly to shorten, if that is possible, the time that most certainly would be taken by such a discussion in the debate on the address.
The question that has come very much to the fore in the last few days is whether there is to be a common policy for all parts of the empire or commonwealth on foreign relations, defence and other matters-a single or common policy as distinct from each nation of the British commonwealth having its own policy on foreign affairs, on defence and on other matters. Let me say at once that, so far as consultation is concerned and cooperation in matters of foreign affairs, defence and the like, as between the different parts of the British empire or the British commonwealth of nations, whichever one prefers to call it, I feel that there cannot be too close consultation and cooperation. I feel that too great an effort cannot be made to ensure careful coordination of these policies, and for my part, wherever opportunity has presented itself in the past or may present itself in the future, I intend to do all that lies within my power to see that there is, among the different nations of the British commonwealth of nations, full consultation, cooperation and coordination, where possible, of all of these particular policies.
I have no very great fear that this consultation and cooperation will not take place. It has steadily grown during the past couple of decades. We have reached to-day an effective method of consultation and cooperation that has not been surpassed at any time in the history of the British empire. It is capable, I believe, in certain particulars, of further development. The whole development, I would say, has been towards perfecting arrangements for effective consultation and cooperation on all matters of eommon interest and concern.
The suggestion of an organization of the relations between the different self-governing parts of the empire or nations of the commonwealth which would help to centralize their activities is not a new one. It has been made time and again over many years in the past, and each time it has come up for consideration some assurance has been given, where it has been dealt with at imperial conferences or meetings of premiers, that the nations of the commonwealth need not fear in the least any invasion of their complete autonomy in shaping their own policies. I should like to give the house in succession the assurances that have been given at different imperial con-

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
ferences. Here may I say that I regret that this question1 should come up at this time, because I do think, involving as it does discussion in the press, in public assemblies and elsewhere, it is to a very considerable extent taking the minds of the people off the immediate thing, which is the winning of the war. Why we need worry to-day about the form of organization which the empire is going to take after the rvar, I cannot understand. I think the thing to-day is to win the war, and when the war is won there will be plenty of time to consider what changes in organization, if any, may be necessary.
Just at this point, lest I should forget it,
. I have been asked the question at different times whether an address which was recently made in Toronto and which dealt with this particular subject had been brought to my attention before it was delivered. I wish to say to the house that I had no knowledge whatever of what was to be said or of what actually was said until after that particular address was made.
Near the close of the last war there was what was known as the imperial war conference of 1917. The suggestion was made by that conference that there should be a meeting for the purpose of considering constitutional relations within the empire. From that day to the present no conference that has been held in Britain lias sought in any way to attempt to form an organization which would deprive in any particular the different legislative bodies of the commonwealth of full control over their own affairs.
The first conference of prime ministers which was held after the war took place in 1921. At that conference-I believe that Canada was represented by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen-the following resolution was passed:
The prime ministers of the United Kingdom and the dominions, having carefully considered the recommendation of the imperial war conference of 1917 that a special imperial conference should be summoned as soon as possible after the war to consider the constitutional relations of the component parts of the empire, have reached the following conclusions:
(a) Continuous consultation to which the prime ministers attach no less importance than the imperial war conference of 1917, can only be secured by a substantial improvement in the communications between the component parts of the empire. Having regard to the constitutional developments since 1917, no advantage is to be gained by holding a constitutional conference.
That was the view taken after the last war, in 1921, that no advantage would be gained by having a conference to deal with these particular questions of constitutional relations within the empire.
The next imperial conference came in 1923.
I was present at that conference, as one of the representatives of Canada. That conference had occasion to deal with questions of foreign relations, communications, signature and ratification of treaties, and matters of defence. The position taken by the conference in these matters is set out very clearly in the following statement, under "Foreign Affairs". After the conference had discussed foreign affairs at some length the statement concludes:
This conference is a conference of representatives of the several governments of the empire; its views and conclusions on foreign policy, as recorded above, are necessarily subject to the action of the governments and parliaments of the various portions of the empire, and it trusts that the results of its deliberations will meet with their approval.
There was this statement with regard to defence:
The conference gave special consideration to the question of defence and the manner in which cooperation and mutual assistance could best be effected, after taking into account the political and geographical conditions of the various parts of the empire.
The conference affirms that it is necessary to provide for the adequate defence of the territories and trade of the several countries comprising the British empire. In this connection the conference expressly recognizes that it is for the parliaments of the several parts of the empire, upon the recommendations of their respective governments, to decide the nature and extent of any action which should be taken by them.
The next conference came in 1926. I was also present at that conference. It was not until 1926 that any conference attempted to develop what might be known as a formula which would set out the existing relations between the different parts of the empire; but at that conference a committee, which was headed by the late Lord Balfour, did present a statement which was adopted by the conference, and which set out in the clearest manner possible the views of the different representatives as to interimperial relations. I read from the report of the conference of 1926:
All the questions on the agenda affecting interimperial relations were referred by the conference to a committee of prime ministers and heads of delegations, of which Lord Balfour was asked to be chairman.
The committee reported as follows:
We were appointed at the meeting of the imperial conference on October 25, 1926, to investigate all the questions on the agenda affectjng interimperial relations. Our discussions on these questions have been long and intricate. We found, on examination, that they involved consideration of fundamental principle* affecting the relations of the various parts of

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
the British empire inter se as well as the relations of each part to foreign countries. For such examination the time at our disposal has been all too short. Yet we hope that we may have laid a foundation on which subsequent conferences may build.
I quote further:
The committee are of the opinion that nothing would be gained by attempting to lay down a constitution for the British empire. Its widely scattered parts have very different characteristics, very different histories, and are at very different stages of evolution: while, considered as a whole, it defies classification and bears no real resemblance to any other political organization which now exists or has ever yet been tried.
There is, however, one most important ele-, ment in it which, from a strictly ponstitutional point of view, has now, as regards vital matters, reached its full development-we refer to the group of self-governing communities composed *of Great Britain and the dominions. Their position and mutual relation may be readily defined. They are autonomous communities within the British empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
And a little further down:
Every self-governing member of the empire is now the master of its destiny.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that no words could be clearer than those in defining the present position; and I must say that the position as thus defined' is the position which this government accepts as the present one and which it desires to see maintained.
In regard to defence:
The conference gave much consideration to the question of defence, and to the methods by which the defence arrangements of each part of the empire could be most effectively coordinated.
In dealing with defence the first item that is set forth is this:
- The resolutions on defence adopted at the last session of the conference are reaffirmed.
The statement there of what was reaffirmed at the previous conference is:
The conference affirms that it is necessary to provide for the adequate defence of the terri, tories and trade of the several countries comprising the British empire. In this connection the conference expressly recognizes that it is for the parliaments of the several parts of the empire, upon the recommendations of their respective governments, to decide the nature and extent of any action which should be taken by them.
There was, I believe, a further conference in 1930 which was attended by Mr. Bennett. I have looked through the proceedings and am unable to see anything which in any way alters the force of the position that was taken at previous conferences in regard to interimperial relations. There was an economic
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
conference which was held in this city in 1932, but it did not touch the question of interimperial constitutional relations. There was a further conference in London in 1937, the year of the coronation. I had again the honour of representing Canada, along with others, at that conference. At that conference foreign affairs, defence and constitutional questions were all on the agenda for discussion. I have a copy of the report of the conference and this is what is stated with respect to foreign affairs and defence. The chairman made the following statement:
Though we shall discuss other important subjects, we are agreed that questions of foreign affairs and defence shall be our main subjects.
During the discussion emphasis was laid on the importance of developing the practice of communication and consultation between different governments as a help to the coordination of policies.
The conference recorded the results of its deliberations on the subject of foreign affairs, and this is the pertinent paragraph:
While no attempt was made to formulate commitments, which in any event could not be made effective until approved and confirmed by the respective parliaments, the representatives of the governments concerned found themselves in close agreement upon a number of general propositions . . . they declared their intention of continuing to consult and cooperate. . . .
And in the matter of defence-
The conference gave close attention to the subject of defence, and considered ways in which it would be possible for the governments concerned to cooperate in measures for their own security.
In the course of the discussions, the conference found general agreement among its members that the security of each of their countries can be increased by cooperation in such matters as the free interchange of information concerning the state of their naval, military and air forces, the continuance of the arrangements already initiated by some of them for concerting the scale of the defences of ports, and measures for cooperation in the defence of communications and other common interests. At the same time the conference recognized that it is the sole responsibility of the several parliaments of the British commonwealth to decide the nature and scope of their own defence policy.
At that conference I made a statement of Canada's position in regard to imperial conferences, and the place that they occupy in settling matters of policy. I will read it to the house because it is the position which, if I were attending a conference of prime ministers later in the year, as I may, I would wish to maintain at that time.
The task of an imperial conference has been well defined as that of considering whethey the several governments represented, while preserving their individual rights of decision and action, can coordinate their various policies in

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
such a way as to assist one another, and help forward the cause of peace. Its function is not to formulate or declare policy. The value of this, as of other imperial conferences, lies mainly in the free exchange of information and opinion; in furnishing the representatives of the several governments with more adequate knowledge of the problems, the difficulties, the aspirations, the attitudes of other members of the British commonwealth of nations; and in giving that direct and immediate understanding of the national and personal factors in the situation which cannot well be obtained by correspondence or indirect communication. With this further knowledge in their possession, the representatives of each government, in consultation with their colleagues and their respective parliaments, are in the best of positions to formulate policies on questions where cooperation is required.
It will be seen that at all the conferences I have mentioned, it was clearly stated that the governments and parliaments of the different countries represented would formulate and decide their own policies, that the conferences were for purposes of consultation to help to make cooperation more effective in the coordinating of policies. It was not for the conferences to formulate policies.
I wonder very much whether those who are speaking about more effective consultation, cooperation and coordination, begin to appreciate how much has been achieved in that direction, how completely there are existing throughout the British commonwealth of nations to-day most effective means of consultation and of cooperation in everything that affects policy, whether it is foreign policy or defence, or communications, or any other particular matter. Let me very quickly mention just what some of those means are.
In the first place there is the communication which takes place between the governments of the different countries. This government receives every day several communications from the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs bringing to our attention matters that are of concern to the different nations of the commonwealth. Our government communicates every day more or less, I think I can say every day, and sometimes sends several messages in a day, to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs giving our views in these matters. There is direct communication between the prime ministers of the different nations of the commonwealth. The Prime Minister of Great Britain communicates direct with the Prime Minister of Canada, as he does with the Prime Minister of Australia and other nations of the commonwealth, and I communicate direct with him or with them when the situation is important enough to have these direct communications in addition to the messages which
are sent through the Department of External Affairs to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs.
Then there is present in Ottawa a representative of the British government in the person of the high commissioner, formerly a very distinguished member of British cabinets. The high commissioner of the United Kingdom is in a position to communicate direct with the members of the government, with myself personally, as he does very frequently, or with officials of the Department of External Affairs, on matters on which it is desirable to have fuller information than that which is likely to come in formal dispatches. But more than that we have also our high commissioner in Great Britain, and our high commissioner is in a position to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister and other ministers of Britain matters on which we feel we should like to give fuller information than is contained in more formal communications. The practice has grown up during the present war of having the high commissioners of all parts of the British empire resident in London meet daily with the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs. He has present with him on most occasions a representative of the foreign office, and at these interviews which take place between the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, who has been sitting in the cabinet at Downing street, there is communicated to the high commissioners what is important in reference to interimperial relations and matters of common concern with respect to the war.
A complete system of representation by high commissioners in different parts of the empire has grown up since the beginning of this war. Canada has had her high commissioner in Britain for many years, and we received the high commissioner from Great Britain for the first time in 1928. Since the outbreak of war, Canada has appointed high commissioners to all the self-governing dominions. We have our high commissioners in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland and Newfoundland. These countries (except Newfoundland) have their high commissioners here in Ottawa.
In addition to that we have ministers or ambassadors in a number of the leading capitals. Our ministers are in touch with the ministers or the ambassadors there from other parts of the commonwealth and are in a position to gather a great deal of information which is communicated to the government at Ottawa, matters of common interest and concern; therefore, in all of these particulars there is from day to day the fullest and most complete kind of consultation.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
I should add that in addition to all of these communications which take place over the wires there are frequent visits by ministers from different nations of the commonwealth, particularly from Great Britain to Canada and frequent visits by our ministers to Great Britain. Scarcely a month goes by that we have not the honour of meeting either here or in Washington or elsewhere a minister of the British government who is on this continent on some important mission. Take the relations between Mr. Churchill and myself. I have had several meetings with Mr. Churchill since the war began, some of them at Washington, some in England and some here in Canada. All of this is a very much changed condition from what existed prior to the war. Means of travel have been so perfected that a minister can cross from Canada to Britain or vice versa in less than a day, and when any question comes up on which we feel it is necessary to have immediate personal consultation we arrange to see that personal consultation is brought about here or overseas.
I should add in addition to that what I think is most important of all, and it is an answer to those who talk about having some imperial council that is going to decide commonwealth policies. We have to-day a continuing conference of cabinet councils of the commonwealth, a continuing conference of cabinets of the commonwealth dealing with matters of common concern. Let me explain what I mean. When any question comes up that is of common concern to the commonwealth in whole or in part, a communication comes, say from London, if that is the source at which the question arises, to our government. A similar communication is sent to the premiers of other goverments of the commonwealth. Immediately I am in a position, as Prime Minister, to take that particular question before my colleagues in the cabinet; and when I give advice to the British government on any matter I am not giving advice by myself alone, in the atmosphere of London, but I am giving advice based on what judgment I am able to form after consulting with the members of the government from all parts of Canada, each of whom has his immediate responsibility to this parliament of Canada which has its responsibility to the people of Canada. I ask: how can conferences between cabinets be carried out more effectively than that?
The objection I have to going over to London to imperial conferences to try to settle policies, if that should be the object, is that I am at a complete disadvantage in those cir-

cumstances; and when I speak of myself it is quite impersonal; I am referring to anyone who holds the office of Prime Minister of Canada. The Prime Minister attending in London meets an entire cabinet. He may be entirely alone. He has not with him all his colleagues; he has with him very few colleagues, unless the business of his own country is to be neglected while he is away. More than that, however, he is without his expert advisers, who are much needed in dealing with great questions of peace or war. On the other hand every minister of the cabinet in London has his expert advisers, when a certain issue is up for discussion, either seated beside him or in an adjoining room, and he is in a position to command their views on any suggestion that may be made. Further, he is in a position to confer with all his colleagues and make his statement to the conference based upon opinions formed in that way. As I say, unless one is prepared to take with him colleagues and experts, and to allow the government of Canada to be carried on minus these responsible ministers and officials while an imperial conference is being conducted, one is not in a position to discuss matters as they should be discussed, and in the light of the responsibilities of the situation, as one would wish to discuss them.	~
But when, as to-day, we have this system under which every question brought up is discussed fully in the cabinets of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Great Britain; when views are interchanged within a very- short time, what more effective means could possibly be found of obtaining a consensus of view, an approach toward common policy, and a coordination of policies? I am one hundred per cent for close consultation, close cooperation and effective coordination of policy on all matters of common concern between the different nations of the British commonwealth. By all means let ub within the British commonwealth be as united as we possibly can in thought and action, but let us seek in regard to other countries also to effect a closer cooperation and coordination of policies, which wall make for the sort of world organization we hope to see prevail in future in this world.

Yes, I prepared this. These are my own views and the views of this government.
A concrete issue in external policy has been raised in recent speeches delivered by Lord Halifax and Field Marshal Smuts. It relates to the domination of certain great powers. Both speeches expressed the view that the future peace of the world depended on the attainment of an equal partnership in strength and influence between the great powers among the united nations. Both took the position that the resources and man-power of the British isles were too small to enable the United Kingdom to compete with the United States and the Soviet Union in power and authority after the war. Both, therefore, argued that it was necessary that the United Kingdom should have the constant support of other countries, in order to preserve a proper balance. Field Marshal Smuts thought that this might be achieved by a close association between the United Kingdom and "the smaller democracies in western Europe"; he had little to say of the place of the British commonwealth as such. Lord Halifax on the other hand declared:
Not Great Britain only, but the British commonwealth and empire, must be the fourth power in that group upon which, under Providence, the peace or the world will henceforth depend.
With what is implied in the argument employed by both these eminent public men I am unable to agree.
It is indeed true beyond question that the peace of the world depends on preserving on the side of peace a large superiority of power, so that those who wish to disturb the peace can have no chance of success. But I must ask whether the best way of attaining this is to seek a balance of strength between three or four'great powers. Should we not, indeed must we not, aim at attaining the necessary superiority of power by creating an effective international system inside which the cooperation of all peace-loving countries is freely sought and given?



The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
It seema to me not to be a matter of matching manpower and resources, or, in other words, military and industrial potential, between three or four dominant states. What we must strive for is close cooperation among those great states themselves, and all other like-minded countries. Behind the conception expressed by Lord Halifax and Field Marshal Smuts there lurks the idea of inevitable rivalry between the great powers. Could Canada, situated as she is geographically between the United States and the Soviet Union, and at the same time a member of the British commonwealth, for one moment give support to such an idea?
The Moscow declaration on general security forecast a system which would involve for its effectiveness, firm commitments by all peace-loving states to do their share in preserving peace. Britain, the United States and the Soviet Union were all represented at the Moscow conference. What would seem now to be suggested is that the prime Canadian commitment should be to pursue in all matters of external relations-"in foreign policy, defence, economic affairs, colonial questions and communications," to cite the words of Lord Halifax -a common policy to be framed and executed by all the governments of the commonwealth. I maintain that apart from all questions as to how that common policy is to be reached, or enforced, such a conception runs counter to the establishment of effective world security, and therefore is opposed to t'he true interests of the commonwealth itself.
We are certainly determined to see the closest collaboration continue between Canada, the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries. Nothing that I am saying should be construed as supporting any other view than this. Collaboration inside the British commonwealth has, and will continue to have, a special degree of intimacy. When, however, it comes to dealing with the great issues which determine peace or war, prosperity or depression, it must not, in aim or method, be exclusive. In meeting world issues of security, employment and social standards we must join not only with commonwealth countries but with all likeminded states, if our purposes and ideals are to prevail. Our commitments on these great issues must be part of a general scheme, whether they be on a world basis or regional in nature.
We look forward, therefore, to close collaboration in the interests of peace not only inside the British commonwealth, but also with all friendly nations, small as well as great.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) kindly consented to my having two or three minutes in which to make a statement.
Evidence is developing that business concerns which are subject to tax at the 100 per

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
cent rate on excess profits are being solicited to make unusually large contributions to various non-profit organizations. The activities of these organizations while in many cases not charitable in the ordinary sense of the word are nevertheless classed as such for tax purposes. These contributions up to a point are allowed as deductions from profits for the purpose of computing tax, and under a 100 per cent tax rate on excess profits the main burden of the gift obviously falls on the dominion treasury and ultimately on the taxpaying public generally rather than on the business concern making the contribution.
It is therefore the intention of the government in the forthcoming budget to recommend to the house a safeguarding measure which will ensure that in the case of any contribution by a business concern, whether corporate or otherwise, to an organization classed as a charitable organization which is subscribed after to-day, that is January 31, 1944, the tax advantage in respect of such contribution shall not be greater than that obtainable by a comparable business concern which is not subject to tax at the 100 per cent rate on excess profits.
For example, in the case of the ordinary commercial or industrial corporation the tax 3 advantage in respect of such contribution will be limited to 40 per cent of such contribution, even if the corporation is subject to tax at the 100 per cent rate on its excess profits.

New Democracy, when war came, stood and stood alone for total use of resources in war. To-day New Democracy stands for total use of the nation's resources when peace comes. It is equally true that fear of international finance will drive the Liberal government and its policies back to where they were before the war, that is to scarcity and limited production in the service of high profits. There cannot be political freedom without economic freedom. There is a tragic lack of both kinds of freedom in the world to-day.
We are fighting the Japs and the Germans in the name of freedom. Let me suggest that in the name of freedom we fight as well our own unjust prejudices; for the lesson of Hitlerism is in vain if it fails to teach us tolerance and generosity. English-speaking democracy under its present leadership has yet to learn that
lesson. Here is crowning evidence to support my statement. Many years ago the Jews, responding to a religious and national, as well as a natural impulse, sought for themselves a new home in their old 'home in Palestine. English-speaking democracy encouraged the Jew to hope; they promised him support. That promise came before the Hitlerian massacres. The Jew, with millions of his countrymen tortured and dead, still hopes and looks to us to make his hopes come true.
Where in democracy are our charity and justice? Where is our Christianity if we let the Jew now hope in vain? I tell this house that the homeless Jew is a challenge to all the decencies that make what we are pleased to call our English-speaking civilization. We dare not refuse that challenge. This house should recognize this truth and this duty by an. appropriate resolution and should give leadership to all nations along the path of justice and fair play through the fulfilment of the long cherished dream of the establishment in Palestine of a national homeland for the Jews.

You can meet the other problem when this country has elected a parliament pledged to put the interests of the people before the claims of international1 finance, pledged to make financially possible what is physically possible and desirable.
Reformers of the capitalistic system, when they speak of the reforms in that system necessary to ensure an equitable distribution of maximum production, are asked how they will do it. It is a question designed to confuse the people, because, when a sensible and sufficient answer is given, I have found that the answer is taken by the technicians of reactionary capitalism and bent and twisted out of its original shape. There is no difficulty in building the machinery which will ensure effective distribution, and I tell the house that the time has gone by when the reactionary capitalists should be able to make people believe that there is any difficulty.
Let me put the matter positively. I defy any member of this house to rise to his feet and say that it is not possible to devise means-whereby to distribute all that the system is able to produce, and to distribute it, too, without adding to the national burden any further debt or taxation, and without imperilling our freedom with regimentation. That challenge stands. Social Credit-New Democracy is not strong in parliament, but it is very strong in the sense that what it stands for is dear to the hearts of the vast majority of Canadians.
The Address-Mr. Blackmore

Social CrediGNew Democracy is not bigoted. It knows that country comes far ahead of party; it also knows very well that there is *but Short time left within which Canadians might effect reforms by the democratic way.
Let us members in this house bear in mind the danger that if the parliament of Canada will not give the people justice, then the people will seek justice in another way in spite of parliament. At this time of crisis it is the responsibility of all men of good will to forget their lesser loyalties, to forget the claims of party and of class, and to join together so that they may defeat the common enemy at borne, even as our soldiers are now joined together to defeat the common enemy abroad. The common enemy abroad is Germany and Japan. The common enemy at home is international finance, special privileges, the kind of big business that chokes the life out of every other kind of business.
It is in this spirit that I appeal to the really progressive members of the Conservative party, and over the heads of the Marxian fanatics and political strategists, I appeal also to the common people of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I appeal to those Liberals who have been able to retain their freedom despite a lifetime of despotic political [DOT]rule. All honour to them! They will be made ^welcome to the company of free men. So let *us get together, forgetful of our minor differences, remembering only that it will take courage and good will on the part of all free men and women to save this country from The chaos which impends.
If my appeal should fall on deaf ears-I trust it will not-then the party of Social Credit-New Democracy will feel in duty bound to go on alone, confident that we shall swiftly grow in strength; for a party which has the honesty and courage to stand against international finance, and for the common man; against socialism, and for reformed private enterprise, in which money will no longer be master; a party which is proud to give its life if needs be in this just cause, is a party which will deserve to have behind it the overwhelming support of a country whose people are still free. Such a party will merit the overwhelming support of the soldiers of Canada; for a party which dared to declare, as this group did, for the total use of the country's resources when this war began, a party which dared to declare for equality of service and equality of sacrifice, should be believed by all of our soldiers when now it declares for the total use of the country's resources when peace shall be restored.
rMr. Blackmore.}
Why did the Liberal government not declare for total war when war began? Its bosses forbade it to do so. Why will the Liberal government not declare for total use of the country's resources now that peace is drawing near? Because its bosses forbid it. And, Mr. Speaker, they are the self-same bosses.
When our soldiers went overseas they imposed upon those who stayed at home a trust. That trust was to build for them a Canada henceforth free from want and unemployment, free from misery and preventable disease, a Canada of real security and happiness. For my part I accepted that trust and I mean to discharge it.
May I turn for a few moments to a consideration of some of the items in the speech from the throne. There arc several things in the speech from the throne which I believe ought to be given special consideration. The government in power has not dealt fairly with agriculture in Canada during the last year. Conditions are gradually improving in agriculture, but it seems to me that the Liberal party has to be forced every step of the way. They do not seem to have a broad, generous, long-range policy; they seem to have a niggardly, cheese-paring policy that concedes a point only grudgingly. I complained of the treatment of the wool producers last spring. The treatment of the lamb producers was a reflection on the intelligence or on the integrity of those who were in charge, and the treatment of the hog situation during this last year has been something to regret; the management of the beef situation casts no honour or credit on the government, while the way in which the beet sugar industry is handled in Canada is a reflection on the government and will be a cause for bitter remorse before this war is over. I do not believe one could persuade any unbiased or dispassionate individual to believe that the men who have had charge of the sugar policy of this country were acting with an eye to the interests of the people of Canada. The labour situation in Canada is far from what it should be. The wartime wages control order, 1943, P.C. 9384, is a most astounding piece of labour legislation bristling with obnoxious features which bear adversely and unfairly upon the workingmen from coast to coast. Our treatment of the returned men is far from reassuring with respect to the future. I find returned men everywhere are dissatisfied. In the first place there has been a removal of the insurance principle from the Pension Act. Very meagre allowances are given to men when they are mustered out of the service, and there is observable indecent haste in the discharge of men from hospital when they are suffering from the results of service.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
The reconstruction and rehabilitation programme of the government is causing apprehension, if not consternation throughout this country. We hear of fine and ambitious plans for post-war rehabilitation but never a solitary word as to where the money is coming from to pay for these plans. Yet the plans are being prepared and promulgated by a government that insistently said before the war, we have not the money. And the same mentalities will commence to think after the war, we have not the money. There is a great deal more than political significance to this matter. It seems to me that the average Liberal, if I gauge him aright, thinks of nothing in the world but whether or not he can get back into power. Whenever a matter comes before him he seems to ask himself, will this particular measure bring me votes? He utterly disregards what may be the effect upon the morale of the country, what may be the effect ultimately upon the welfare of the Canadian people.
We hear a great deal about the conversion of war-time industries to peace-time uses. I believe the hon. Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) gave a rather impressive speech somewhere in the east in November, if I remember correctly. In that speech he said there was no reason at all why anyone should be unemployed in Canada after the war. I agree with him. There has been no reason why anyone should be unemployed in Canada since 1930. There certainly was no reason after 1935. But that does not deal wdth the matter at all. I will grant that we can easily reconvert munition plants in the main and prepare them to produce peace-time goods. The great question is, how in the world are you going to enable the people to buy the goods when they are produced? I am informed we had in Canada in 1939 a production of around three and a half billion dollars, and that during 1943 that production rose to roughly eight billion dollars. We are buying in the neighbourhood of $4,000,000,000 worth of goods with the taxpayers' money and with the money we borrow, and are giving it away. What are we to be doing after the war to correspond with the gifts we are so munificently conferring upon Hitler and the Japanese? I suppose if anyone were to suggest to anyone in this house that we could give $25 a month or something like that he would probably have nightmares for three nights or more. But that does not seem to disturb the mentality of those Canadians who are giving many times that amount to the enemy. The all-important problem after the war will be the selling of the goods. The government steers clear of that problem. I suppose government members will answer me immediately
and say, we are planning on export trade markets. Let it be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, that when the war closes there will be sixty nations in this world all seeking for export markets, each one trying to sell more than it buys. Does the Liberal mentality find it impossible to conceive the absolute grotesqueness of that situation, or does it conceive that Canada, because of her economic strength, is going to be able to crow'd the other nations out of the markets and lay the foundation for another war? If everyone of those sixty nations operates under the system in vogue in Canada it will have a shortage of purchasing power within the nation which will be its most painful disability. Canada in this respect will be one of the foremost among them.
Until we learn how to adjust that shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people, all talk of reorganizing the world on a peaceful basis is utterly idle.
In the speech from the throne we have the proposal to import goods in order to raise our standard of living. May I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the first task of the government is to enable the Canadian people to buy the goods that Canada can produce, buy a sufficient amount of them to raise their standard of living to the point where it should be. We should enable them to buy grains and grain products, vegetables, fruits, animal products and coal, building material and furni-. turn, shoes, clothing and machinery. All these things we produce abundantly in Canada. Why not arrange matters so that our people will be able to buy all they need of these things? Think what it would mean in this * country, a land literally flowing with milk and honey, if every Canadian were given by this parliament the assurance that, if he cooperated, never again would he go in need of the food, clothing, shelter, culture, education and recreatioa that Canada's fields and mines, her waters, forests and workshops stand ready to provide for him abundantly-if only he has the money with which to buy? Supply Canadians with purchasing power with which to buy their own goods and they will buy the imports they need; the government will not have to worry about imports at all.
Now I come to these social security proposals. The whole system offered by the government is merely a plan to tax Canadians into prosperity; no people can tax themselves into prosperity. The whole scheme constitutes an ambitious attempt to redistribute scarcity. There is no evidence of an expanding economy or that such has been contemplated. Such measures offer no possible means for attaining the total use of resources. Expand-
The Address-Mr. Caldwell

ing economy and total use of resources can be achieved only through the employment of debtr-free money. I submit once more to this house that the all-important thing for us to consider at this time is the feasibility of debt-free money with which we can cancel the debt which accumulates in this debt-creating system of ours, debt-free money with which we can distribute the abundance which God has given us the capacity to produce.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
(Rosetown-Big-gar): Mr. Speaker, first allow me to join with those who have already extended congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address, for their two interesting and able speeches. I want to deal tonight with a few problems which confront the Canadian people, but before doing so I should like to refer to the speech delivered this afternoon by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). I want to say at once that I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he suggests that the place for the leader of a political party is in this house. I venture to say that if Mr. John Bracken were to walk down the corridors of this building most of the members of this house would not recognize him, though he has been leader of the Progressive Conservative party for some fourteen months now. It is not that he has not had the opportunity, had he chosen to take it, of seeking a seat here. Sitting beside and behind me to-night are two new members from western Canada, both farmers representing rural [DOT] seats, one of them almost within a stone's throw of the legislative building where Mr. John Bracken has occupied a seat for twenty years. Had he chosen to avail himself of it the opportunity was there for him to try his luck, if you will, in obtaining a seat in this house, as he should have done; but of course, in spite of the boasting of the Progressive Conservative party, I would remind them that the provincial seat of The Pas, in the Manitoba provincial legislature, which was occupied for so long by Mr. John Bracken, was lost by his followers in that province, and that all the candidates in that by-election lost their deposit to the successful Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidate.
I do not propose to comment upon what has been said this evening by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). As I listened to him I was reminded of a verse which I have read, which runs, something like this: "I thank God I am not as other men."
I should like immediately to express the thankfulness which we share with all the people of Canada for the brightening prospects of 
a military victory in Europe, and for the preparations that have been made to overcome Japanese aggression. However, events in Italy and in New Guinea during the past few days warn us that we have a long and perhaps bloody road ahead. On our home front I think we ought to pay tribute to the splendid selfsacrifice of our farmers and their families and the efforts of the thousands of workers and office personnel who have produced vast quantities of food and material to back the attack. The achievements of women in many fields in Canada, too, have been no less striking than those to which I have just referred. Overseas the bravery, skill and fighting qualities of our service men and women are bringing results of which this nation may well be proud. Nor must we overlook the contribution of those who organized and trained the forces. Particularly may I mention the services of Lieutenant-General McNaughton, who was among the first in our commonwealth to prepare his army corps for the type of mechanized, scientific warfare which this great conflict has come to be. A fuller explanation of his recent retirement than has yet been given is awaited by both service personnel and large groups of our civilian population.
In spite of our military achievements, however, many Canadians have grave misgivings in regard to the future. The prosecution of the war and the shaping of post-war policy are inseparably bound together. Military and political warfare are inseparable parts of the same struggle for security and freedom. There is a grave danger that while we may be victorious on the field of battle we may lose the no less vital political warfare. There are ominous signs that attempts are being made to appease the fascists and reactionary groups that stand for a return to the pre-war status quo throughout the world. For months Franco has been placated, while he has maintained a division of men fighting our allies on the eastern European front. In Italy we have bolstered a discredited monarch and a former fascist general, while progressive Italians demand the formation of a government in which the Italian people can have confidence, under whose leadership the Italians could fight the common enemy. Throughout Europe, we are told, the courageous underground workers lack confidence in our intentions, as we continue to support discredited governing cliques and former monarchs who are obviously distrusted and disliked by their former subjects. Expediency may be the name but reaction is the substance. Nor can Canada escape some responsibility for this disastrous appeasement. As the fifth among the united nations, or first,

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
if you will, among the so-called smaller nations, Canada should exercise an influence commensurate with her military and economic power. Her failure to do so invites the judgment that our government is afraid of the social and economic implications of democracy at home and abroad. It is high time that our external relationships were brought under careful review by this parliament. It is time that we stripped some of the unnecessary secrecy that surrounds some of our foreign policy. I earnestly suggest that the standing committee on industrial and international relations- uneasy bedfellows-be split up into two committees, one concerned with labour and the other with international affairs. We need an informed public opinion to support intelligent national policies in these fields.
The speech from the throne states that the well-being of Canada is bound up with the restoration and recovery of world trade. While that is true, we must not allow a government to rely solely upon such trade for our own post-war recovery and well-being. Certainly the speech reveals little understanding of the means by which trade can be expanded in this modern world. As a first principle I suggest that the orderly planning of our internal economy is vital to domestic prosperity and to our ability to trade effectively; for effective trade surely means that we must accept and use the products of other countries in order that we may dispose of our own surpluses abroad.	,
There is no indication in the speech from the throne that the government appreciates the need of introducing planning into our trade relationships with other countries, as well as into our internal economy. Has our wartime experience of trade through government agencies taught us nothing? How can we plan trade on the basis of national need? Surely through the adaptation of methods of the bulk purchases and sales made now by national agencies. It is clear that bulk buying and selling on a national scale is surely foreshadowed by several nations including our own best customer, Great Britain. If we fail to use such boards as the bacon board and the wheat board, instead of reopening all kinds of private and speculative agencies, our foreign trade will languish. Perchance it will be strangled by a veritable jungle of tariffs, quotas, irresponsible cartels and emergency policies.
The speech from the throne, however, shows that the government has stolen some ideas from the C.C.F. programme. Unfortunately it is only petty larceny of which I can find it guilty. I wish it were of the grander
sort; for, after all, its social security programme lacks the necessary basis to sustain it. It suggests the building of a superstructure without laying the foundation of full employment, productivity and the actual means of distribution.
The central problem of our time is that of full employment. Social security measures, essential as they are, must remain inadequate until this central problem of full employment is solved. If we fail to make plans by which alone full employment can be obtained, the burden of new social security measures will fall upon the workers and farmers. The government fails to realize that fundamental economic and social change is the price of social security and of economic freedom. But even the social security measures proposed in the speech from the throne are not firm commitments. A study of the language used filled me, I must confess, with the suspicion that it was merely a pre-election document. If the government means what it seems to imply, let it put its programme on the statute books this session, and into full effect, before going to the country. The people are suspicious of death-bed repentances. They showed that in 1935, as our Conservative friends will remember.
And the Liberal party has, I submit, a bad record of neglected promises. Let me remind the house that.-in 1919, now a quarter of a century ago the Liberal party promised the people of Cam.da, among other things-and I shall quote (he exact words:
An adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability.
Now, after twenty-five years, with a spectacular loss of support across the country, it repeats its promise of long ago.
In all these years, what have we got?-an inadequate unemployment scheme in 1938, and some pre-death loans, called old age pensions. Therefore, when the speech from the throne says-and again I quote-
... a national minimum of social security and human welfare should be advanced as rapidly as possible-
-we in this house have a duty to demand: How soon? Another twenty-five years, perhaps. Actual legislation this session, before an election, is the only answer the house should tolerate.
But again I say all the social security measures contained in the speech from the throne leave untouched the central problems of our time, the problems of full employment and the proper distribution of goods and services. Furthermore, this scheme of social security cannot be achieved without an immeso
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

diate attempt to solve the grave constitutional difficulties of which we are all aware. These the present government has shelved and shirked.
A few years ago the dominion, and all but one of the provinces, had Liberal governments. Yet, no solution was found, even when the governments were basically as a party in agreement. How does the government face up to the constitutional problems now? Here is what the speech from the throne says:
.	.	. the working out of a comprehensive
national scheme, in which federal and provincial activities will be integrated and which will include nation-wide health insurance, will require further consultation and close cooperation with the provinces.
And then, note this:
My ministers will welcome opportunities for such consultation.
To use a slang expression, surely that is a prize example of passing the buck.
.No, that will not do. In the absence of an immediate dominion-provincial agreement, let this parliament enact the measure and invite the provinces to cooperate, much as we did in the case of old age pensions.
Those with good memories will recall a somewhat similar statement to the one 1 quoted from the speech from the throne a moment ago, one which was made by the present Prime Minister in April, 1930, when the depression was deepening. He said, as recorded in Hansard for that year, at page 1226:
In the absence of any representations indicating that there is an unemployment situation which the provinces cannot cope with, we have no right to say that there is any national unemployment situation in this country.
The time has come surely when the national government must assume the initiative in matters vital to the well-being of Canada. Above all, then, we urge the government to take action now. This social security programme, which the C.O.F. has done so much to popularize across the country during past years, is badly overdue. Other countries have had much of it for several generations. But again I warn that social security measures, desirable and necessary as they are, do not even pretend to solve the central problem of full employment.
Remember, that the present unemployment insurance fund, though nearly $180,000,000, would be a mere drop in the bucket if we failed to provide full employment for the million persons now employed in war industries, and the nearly 800,000 engaged in the armed services. The fund would only provide benefits for all those for less than eight weeks.

To rely upon social security measures to meet the post-war problem of full employment is in our opinion to court disaster. Therefore the proposals in the speech if put into effect, and they must be, can give only limited financial protection against a calamity which the government proposes nothing effective to prevent. On top of that it is questionable how much social security can be financed while the basic economic and monetary issues remain untouched. The truth is, of course, that health is more important that health insurance; work more important than unemployment insurance; rehabilitation more important than disability pensions; decent incomes and good homes more important than family allowances; independence more important than a dole. Health, work, rehabilitation, decent incomes, good homes, economic planning and social independence are the demands of the Canadian people, more particularly the demands of our sons and our daughters fighting the battles overseas. Yet the speech from the throne offers nothing to achieve these ends, so I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) an amendment to the amendment as follows:
That all the words of the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that in the opinion of this house Your Excellency's advisers have failed to propose the fundamental social changes and economic planning which alone can hasten the winning of the war and make possible the establishment of a post-war Canada capable of providing full employment and complete social security."
The only positive approach to an economic problem to be found in the speech from the throne is the government's promise of aid to certain types of business, presumably in the hope that some crumbs may reach the people. We are told that there is to be an industrial development bank. Instead of bringing the banking, financial and monetary system under sooial ownership and control, the government proposes to establish a new institution which is apparently to assume the most risky and unprofitable part of the post-war credit operations. Instead of a financial system operating solely for the Canadian people, a new government bank is to be set up whose sole aim apparently is to aid certain types of private business.
For generations some of the leaders of the Liberal party-and I remember specifically the former Minister of Finance, the Hon. C. A. Dunning-urged the creation of an agricultural bank to assist our most neglected industry, but without avail. What agriculture asked for years ago, some businesses are about to get.

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
The farmer is offered a price floor for staple farm products. What sort of floor and for what staple products? True, the C.C.F. has popularized the demand for a floor under farm prices, but any price floor must be related to the cost of the things the farmer buys and uses. In other words it must be a parity price, not a price which is merely a low minimum and out of relation to other prices. Again I warn that a parity price depends upon the extent to which the country is able to plan its economy. In other words parity prices like full employment depend upon our willingness to make fundamental economic changes. That the government and the official opposition will not do. Evidence of this unwillingness is to be found in various phrases in the speech from the throne.
We learn that there are to be "suitable tax modifications." If this means, as I rather suspect, reduction in the excess profits taxes or corporation taxes or taxes in the hig ler income brackets, then we shall strenuously oppose such measures. If on the other hand it means the release of purchasing power through the reduction of taxation in the lower brackets we shall be prepared to support it.
The C.C.F. contends that big business has profited too much out of this war, not too little. It may profit more through the activities of the new War Assets Corporation. This body will dispose of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of publicly-owned plant and machines, tools, stores, equipment and material, all at salvage prices. The cry goes up that the government-owned plants will be of little value when the war ends. Private business demands that they be disposed of so that their vested interests shall not be jeopardized. To my mind every effort should be made to utilize these plants to give more employment, more goods and services to the Canadian people. The policy of the government in this regard is the direct opposite to intelligent *economic planning and to the needs and I believe the will of the Canadian people.
How improvident this sort of policy is can be illustrated* by the announcement made in the house last Friday by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). For reasons not disclosed the government has expropriated the properties of the Eldorado Mining Corporation at a price of $1.35 a share, which incidentally is above the price of the stock quoted in Toronto last Friday. In justice to the foresight of our late leader, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, it should be recalled that in May, 1932, Mr. Woodsworth urged that the valuable radium deposits on Great Bear lake should be brought under public ownership and dedicated to human welfare. He
stated that if we were to desire the property in the future we would pay a high price to the promoters whereas at that time the only man with a just claim was the prospector. His words were ignored, and so to-day expropriation will cost the people of Canada some millions of dollars. As I have said already, the price paid by the government is higher than the market value of the stock the day the deal was announced to this house.
The speech from the throne when taken in conjunction with the record of the government gives us little hope for effective measures to cope with the stupendous problems of the future. What the country needs is a definite and specific programme, not vague promises which is almost all the speech from the throne contains. The C.C.F. has committed itself to a full social security programme. What we have also done, and other parties have failed to do, is to provide the economic basis which will make such a programme possible and feasible. What should such a programme contain? First, this parliament should suggest a sum which the country is prepared to spend in the immediate post-war period. Last year, and I repeat the suggestion, I urged that we name five billion dollars as the target of expenditure in the first two years following victory.
First, there must be a concrete, comprehensive and good post-war housing programme instead of the pitiful nibbling at the problem suggested in the throne speech. We should state immediately that we will spend at least $500 million a year to provide adequate houses in town and country for the Canadian people. This vast opportunity to bring decency and comfort to every Canadian and to eliminate overcrowding and squalor is a challenge that we can meet only by the boldest attack. This of course is a means also of providing useful employment for thousands in many branches of industry.
Next must come a plan for rural electrification, to bring modem conveniences to every home in the country. Such a programme would lighten the burdens of rural life, raise standards of living, and-again-provide employment. Next comes the essential task of reestablishment of our service personnel. The reference to this in the speech from the throne is distinctly disturbing. Apparently the government views with satisfaction and complacency the totally inadequate measures already provided. I quote the words of the speech:
A broad programme has already been developed for the reestablishment of veterans of the present war, and for the care of disabled veterans and the dependents of our fighting men and merchant seamen.
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

During the period of demobilization the armed service personnel should be kept on full pay and allowances until they are absorbed permanently in remunerative employment. This is one promise that we must make now and carry out for the men and women in the services. Government-owned plants set up for the purpose of war production should be retained under public ownership and converted to peace-time production. Farm implements and supplies, prefabricated houses, commercial aeroplanes and other desirable goods could be produced in these plants. In fact, the farm cooperatives in the west are anxious to go into the production of some of these things. We should immediately make it possible for these cooperatives to acquire the necessary plant and should also make available to them credit for this purpose.
There is still room in Canada for great economic expansion, particularly in the Canadian north. This should be a planned public post-war development. Surveys made in Canada, particularly in regard to oil possibilities, and the experience of the Soviet Union in the development of similar territory, indicate there may be vast natural resources in Canada waiting to be tapped.
Another new field particularly suitable for western Canada is that of chemurgy. Organized research should be undertaken with a view to discovering and developing new uses for agricultural products.
Perhaps one of the most essential things is that we should immediately appropriate a large sum of money for the expansion of the work of the national research council and other public research groups. It is vital to retain for the public benefit the services of the scientists now engaged in research activities. This involves for them adequate remuneration and security. We have watched some of these brilliant young scientists enter the service of the research council, be kept on a pittance doing the scientific work for several years, and then picked up by some industry, given a laboratory, a good salary, and security; their brains, their skills and their inventive genius sometimes lost to the people of Canada and acquired by a private corporation. To my mind the remuneration given to the young scientists who have done so much in this war, under our research council, is nothing short of a public scandal.
All this necessitates, of course, the investment and expenditure of money. Thus since the charters of the banks are due for renewal the government should introduce legislation to bring the chartered banks under public ownership and control. This should be accom-

panied by a national investment board to direct savings into socially desirable channels; and who is there who will rise in his place and say that a government-owned banking system would not be infinitely safer than the privately-owned chartered banks were in 1931 and 1932 when the finance act of this country had to be amended by order in council to allow some of the banks to deposit securities otherwise not depositable, in order to get the necessary funds to meet their obligations to the public? Or who will say that a national investment board directing the savings of the people would not give more ample security to the people of Canada than the present speculative system under which we live?

The national executive of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation endorses the statement which our federal leader, Mr. M. J. Coldwell, made public with regard to the recent proposals of Lord Halifax. Those proposals are unacceptable, not only because they are against the interests of Canada, but also because they are against the best interests of Britain, of the commonwealth, and of *world peace. The principles underlying these proposals seem to be empire isolationism and power politics. Such assumptions are contrary to the principles of the Atlantic charter. They are the present-day version of pre-war Tory foreign policy.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes that Britain with the other nations of the commonwealth can and should play a leading part in the establishment of the necessary international order after victory. Further, we believe that Britain herself has now an unprecedented opportunity of assuming a position of leadership in the world's march toward enduring peace based on collective security and international economic cooperation. Canada should at all times give full support to a policy which, based on the principles of the Atlantic cl nrter, will win the cooperation not only of the members of the commonwealth but equally <1 all other small and great peace-loving nations. Tile future international order, if it is to endure, must not be based on power groups, imd least of all on domination by a few great powers, but on full participation by all states in the processes of peace building andi in the machinery of political and economic cooperation.
This is the kind of foreign policy which the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes Canada and other members of the British commonwealth should pursue.
