Thank you, sir.
Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauhamois-
Laprairie (Translation): Mr. Speaker, the few remarks which I intend to make in connection with the speech from the throne will not be lengthy. We shall have at some future moment an opportunity to discuss the various measures announced as soon as they are introduced and better understood.
Let us note first that the speech from the throne does not foreshadow an early end of the hostilities, and that, on the other hand, it gives us to understand that the Canadian people will be called upon to achieve a still greater war effort, especially through the extension to the United Nations of the mutual aid principle, which was at the outset a veiled formula used in describing the gift of billions of dollars to England.
I have already condemned and I still condemn such free gifts to a country that is wealthier than ours and more interested in the present conflict. I have condemned and I still condemn Canada's war effort, which is out of proportion with our resources. I said last year, and I repeat this year, that I cannot understand, in view of our geographical position, far from the scene of the conflict, with no possessions to protect outside America, that the chief aim assigned to Canada by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should be a war effort proportionately greater than that of any other allied country, regardless of post-war consequences.
On his return from a trip to England, in November last, the honourable the minister of munitions (Mr. Howe) told us again of the amazement with which our war effort was looked upon over there, and he explained how profitable it was for us to supply as an outright. gift the goods delivered to Great Britain, in order that we might retain the British market after the war.
Around the same time, unfortunately for our minister, the agricultural advisor of the British Embassy in Washington implied that after the war, England would buy her bacon from Denmark in exchange for her industrial products; Denmark, however, presented England with no gifts whatsoever, nor did she give her, simply as a donation, any of her merchandise.
On the other hand, according to a dispatch from London dated January 18th, Sir John Anderson informed the House of Commons that Great Britain would pay cash for some of her purchases in the United States.
They should stop trying to fool us so as to justify our gifts to a country wealthier than ours. After the war, England will act in her
The Address-Mr. Raymond

own interests. That is what we should do also.
In this war we have played and still play the part of a servant who is not consulted but who must take marching orders. London dictates, pledges herself, and we pay the price by going to ruin, and the Prime Minister is happy!
A few days ago, Lord Halifax paid us a visit to tell us what we should do after the war to safeguard the Empire's possessions. He forgets that we are living in America and that we are a neighbour of the United States. May I say that the policy of the Bloc Popu-Iaire Canadien takes its inspiration from this formula of Lord Tweedsmuir: "A Canadian owes his first allegiance not to the British Commonwealth, but to Canada". And we will act in our own interests, which happen to be in America.
For the first time since the declaration of war, the government seems to show some concern for the future. It is behind England, however, who gave that subject plenty of thought when the war had barely begun. The speech from the throne, as a matter of fact, is very promising, and in the field of promises, it even goes beyond the social reforms programme proclaimed sensationally by Lord Bennett, just before general elections in 1935. A sure sign that elections are coming.
Several social measures are announced. In the first place, we wish to go on record as opposing any encroachment upon the provincial rights, and we shall demand that in the enforcement of the laws provincial autonomy be fully respected.
In reading the speech from the throne, certain passages are noted which deserve particular attention. Thus, the government informs us that its ministers are determined, insofar as possible, to provide for the future. This is an admission that they had not up to now given any thought to the future of our people. Unfortunately we were too w'ell aware of this.
Further, it is stated:
The family and the home are the foundation of national life. To aid in ensuring a minimum of well-being to the children of the nation and to help gain for them a closer approach to equality of opportunity in the battle of life, you will be asked to approve a measure making provision for family allowances.
What a discovery on the part of the government! The Bloc Populaire Canadien deserves perhaps a share of credit for the announcement of this reform, inasmuch as since its formation, a year and a half ago, the welfare' of the family headed our programme.
[Mr. Raymond.*
Most of the social reforms announced were sorely needed'. I have long been advocating in this house, on behalf of the working man, a living wage,, a healthy home, means of properly bringing up his family, in a word social welfare legislation.
I shall confine myself to recalling my interventions on behalf of textile workers. The Turgeon investigation ordered by the government had revealed an intolerable situation. As the report was pigeonholed, in 1939, I called the attention, of the government to the recommendations of the investigating commissioner in order to remedy the situation and proposed a bill to implement the recommendations. The government managed to prevent it from going through the required readings. This is the concern which the government has shown for the working man.
From 1930 to 1939, the Bennett and King governments meted out direct relief to the people to prevent them from dying of hunger. From 1939 to this day, the war has filled the bill and for the post-war period, a taxation formula is being worked out to pay for the gifts we have handed out to nations wealthier than we are. To-day, it is sought, by new promises, to help forget past promises -that went unfulfilled; such a scheme does not work any more.
No matter how worthy the reforms proposed in the speech from the throne, one fact remains; it is that the government does not enjoy public confidence to such a degree that it could put them into effect. A proof of this statement is to be found in the result of the four by-elections held last August, when the candidates of the government were defeated in each of the four constituencies. Our people have had enough of unfulfilled promises. New promises on the eve of an election will not have the effect of restoring confidence in the present government.
Last year, when the Prime Minister blamed me for severing my connections with the Liberal party, he said that I did not do honour to the province of Quebec. I answered that, when the time would come for me to get the approval of the voters of Quebec, I would not dread their verdict.
The test has been taken in Stanstead and Montreal-Cartier, and you know the result.. The government candidates were overwhelmed by' the standard-bearers of the Bloc Populaire Canadien, in spite of the fraud resorted to by government officials.
In Montreal-Cartier, the Bloc Populaire candidate crushed the government nominee, and if the Labour-Progressive candidate polled 150 votes more than our man, it is only because thousands of fictitious names had been added

The Address-Mr. Raymond
to the voters' lists and other thousands of voters had been deprived1 of their electoral rights. The Labour-Progressive candidate was permitted to name enumerators to revise the lists while the Bloc Populaire representative was denied t'he same privilege. A royal enquiry should be held, for the parties responsible were in the pay of the government.
In a speech delivered in September last before the National Liberal Federation, the Prime Minister attacked the Bloc Populaire. It happened after the by-elections held in Stanstead and Montreal-Cartier, in the province of Quebec.
He claimed that our group had but a negative and destructive doctrine, that it was attempting to raise Quebec against the other provinces in order to win votes and secure influence by appeals to race prejudice. And hfe pictured us as a danger to Canadian unity.
His grounds for complaint should be noted. Our doctrine was negative and destructive, he said. Where does he find that? The Bloc Populaire was formed in September 1942. In my first address, delivered in October 1912, 1 stated as a principle that Canada, being a Christian country, should be governed like a Christian country, that our first concern would be the people. Consequently, we advocated a policy designed to protect and help the Christian family and its numerous children, and to facilitate their education and employment.
I advocated special consideration for public health, the elimination of slums, and a readjustment of salaries, so that our people might live under healthful conditions, and the heads of families might give adequate shelter and food to their children. I also advocated a revision of the taxation system that would take care of large families. Instead of increasing the tax burden which large families have to bear, we would have lightened it. We wanted and we still want, in short, to safeguard the family, which is the foundation of society.
How can the Prime Minister find anything destructive in such a policy? The speech from the throne even seems to have taken a leaf out of it.
In the field of foreign policy, we demand, for Canada, true sovereignty and the attributes of a sovereign state; true provincial autonomy; we demand a national anthem, a national flag, as all other dominions of the commonwealth; we demand that the Governor of Canada be a citizen of the country as in other dominions; we demand the discontinuance of appeals to the Privy Council and of recourse to the Westminster parliament in matters of amendments to the constitution.
We wish to make of Canada a truly sovereign nation.
I could keep this nomenclature up indefinitely but I refer you to the Bloc's programme which has been made public.
The Prime Minister added that the Bloc Populaire was attempting to raise Quebec against the other provinces in fomenting racial prejudice. It would be truer to state that it was the Prime Minister who attempted, on this occasion, to raise the other provinces against Quebec.	'
Is demanding that the constitution be adhered to and that Quebec be represented as it should, equivalent to raising the other provinces against Quebec or fomenting racial prejudice. If so, Mr. Godbout, who, last year, protested against the procedure of the Government in connection with the redistribution of seats, would be as much to blame as we are.
Is protesting against conscription equivalent to raising the other provinces against Quebec? Then the Prime Minister would have been guilty of the same crime in 1917, when he was opposing conscription while all provinces except Quebec were clamoring for it.
Is demanding that the rights of minorities be respected as guaranteed by the constitution, that provincial autonomy be not infringed upon, that we enjoy our legitimate share of government appointments, that the workers of Quebec receive wages commensurate with those paid in Ontario, equivalent to fomenting racial prejudice?
We have become accustomed to hearing the Prime Minister make an appeal for national unity every time he requests concessions on our part.
Our policy is clear and unequivocal. Our movement is national in its principles and it will remain national in its manifestations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish to follow the tradition of congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address; but they will understand that I cannot agree with all that they said.
During the recess we have witnessed many important happenings, some of them having to do with our national life and others being closely connected with our external policy. One of the most important, beyond doubt, was the Quebec conference in August, 1943. I wish to offer the government my congratulations upon having chosen the city of Quebec, my own city, as the scene of this conference. I do not hesitate to say that the people of Quebec appreciated the choice of
The Address-Mr. Dorion

their capital for the holding of this historic meeting. I am sure that our visitors had an opportunity of getting to know our people and of learning that notwithstanding certain misinformation spread by some parts of the press, the people of the province of Quebec are as loyal as anyone else and especially as Canadian as anyone else. This conference also gave the people of Quebec an opportunity to manifest their fullest appreciation of those who, coming from abroad, do not attempt to overawe them or treat them as inferiors, as unfortunately happens much too often, but come as gentlemen. This appreciation extends particularly to the British Prime Minister and his colleagues. It was a great pleasure for our people to hear Mr. Churchill, his distinguished wife and charming daughter, speak to them fluently in their own language. I am sure that no one in Quebec will forget the speech delivered by Miss Churchill over the radio on August 27, when she said:
Je me rejouirai toujours d'etre descendue d'abord a Quebec. C'est ainsi qu'il faut arriver au Canada.
This may be translated: "I will always be delighted to have come down first to Quebec. It is the way one must come into Canada." But I must say, Mr. Speaker, that if our people were happy to receive such important personages, at the same time they were very sorry to notice the insignificant role played in this conference by our own government. Once more it was evident that our country does not possess the international status which would put it on the same footing as the other nations.
Another very important event I should like to recall is the appointment of Mr. Justice Thibaudeau Rinfret as chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. No doubt the government deserves our congratulations on this appointment, because Judge Rinfret was surely the man best qualified to fill such an important post. I am sure the people as a whole, as well as lawyers and others who have anything to do with the Supreme Court of Canada, learned of this appointment with great satisfaction.
Another event occurred which was not so important of itself but which became of some significance because of the declarations made on that occasion. I refer to the Liberal caucus held in Ottawa in September of last year. According to a report published in the Ottawa Evening Journal of September 28 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), addressing his friends of the Liberal party said, as he did this afternoon, that probably no general election would take place before the end of the war; but he added that some circumstances fMr. Dorion.)
might force the government to appeal to the country sooner. Among those circumstances was the following: any one of the opposition groups, or a combination of them, being able
so to impede the progress of business in parliament, or so misrepresenting and distorting government policy, as to make it next to impossible to carry on. I do not know if by this statement the Prime Minister intended to prevent the opposition groups from criticizing the government, but. if he did I think he made a mistake. On this point I should like to quote from an address delivered some time ago by the ex-president of the Canadian Bar Association:
Executive control of speech, particularly of speech in criticism of the executive, is fundamentally and completely incompatible with free institutions, whether the criticism be directed against the personnel,, policies or acts of that executive or of any board or commission appointed by it. In time of war everyone will recognize the propriety of restricting the dissemination of certain types of information or even of banning the expression of views calculated to injure the country's cause; but to attempt to ban or restrict criticism, however injudicious, of the conduct of the executive or its agencies, is an assault on the very citadel of freedom and the establishment in the seats of power of its deadliest enemy. After all, there are some principles the preservation of which is more important than the fate of any government.
I believe everyone who is interested in the safeguarding of democracy and of our parliamentary system must hold the same views.
The only other event I should like to mention is the result of the by-elections that took place in our province last August. Once more the government has been defeated and has been shown that it has lost the confidence of the people. The result of the elections in Stanstead and Cartier demonstrated that the opinion of the people of Quebec was the same in 1943 as it was in 1942, when I was elected for Charlevoix-Saguenay. These three by-elections in my province give evidence that the Liberal party has lost its grip on that province. This does not mean that any other political group would do much better, because knowing quite well the sentiment of our people I am sure I am right when I repeat what I said last session, that having been tossed for seventy-five years between "reds" and "blues" only to serve as stepping stones to power, without any advantage to themselves, the people of Quebec have become wary; and, though not sure of the political orientation they will ultimately adopt, have decided for the present to support men who, having broken with old ties, can offer them guarantees of sincerity and above all, unselfishness.

The Address-Mr. Dorion
I just said, Mr. Speaker, that the byelections in Quebec in 1943 proved abundantly that this government does not represent the sentiment of the people of Quebec or of the country. To support that statement I- should like to recall a declaration made by the Prime Minister himself on January 29, 1934, When he was leader of the opposition, and I quote from page 34 of Hansard for that year:
So the evidence from every side goes to prove that not only has the government lost the confidence of the country but it has lost confidence in itself. _ May I state further that no matter what majority it may have as a result of the number of hon. members returned at the time the government came into office, that majority no longer represents the opinion of the Canadian people. By-elections have expressed in no uncertain voice the opinion of our people. This government has lost the moral authority to govern. . . .
I repeat the statement. I say that having lost by-election after by-election in all parts of Canada during the last two or three years and the people having spoken so positively and so emphatically, it lias been made perfectly plain that the gouvemment has lost the moral authority to govern, and if it followed its duty it would resign, go to the people and allow them to speak. The Canadian people as a whole should be given an opportunity at a general election to express their view upon policies which up to the present they have been able to do only in part in by-elections.
I have no doubt that if the Prime Minister was right in 1934 we should not be too long to-day in repeating his own words; and a statement like this weighs more heavily on the eve of the very important journey which the Prime Minister is about to undertake. If we refer to statements made lately by most important statesmen, especially to the address delivered a few days ago in Toronto by Viscount Halifax, it is certain that at the next imperial conference there will be some discussions of very great interest for our country, and there may be some decisions which will bind the future of Canada. Is it logical, is it democratic when all the other prime ministers who will attend this meeting have received fresh mandates from their constituents-is it fair for the people of Canada to have, as their representative, the head of a political party which, according to his own words, does not represent any more the sentiment of the people. It may happen that in such a state of affairs Canadians will not consider themselves bound by the decisions emanating from this [DOT] conference.
It is true that we have a very fine speech from the throne, a speech which gives contentment to members of the Liberal party. But this is surely not enough to give the government authority to speak for the people of Canada. There will be much to say about the speech from the throne, and no doubt during the session we shall have an opportunity of
discussing in detail the legislation which will come out of it. I hope the government will submit to the house the measures announced in the speech, so that we can give them careful study. I hope, also, that all these measures will be discussed on their own merits with the greatest possible broad-mindedness, and that it will not give to anyone the occasion to raise discrimination against one province or another.
As regards our international policy, we heard not long ago that the government had decided to name ambassadors to some countries. There is no doubt that these nominations constitute another push, leading Canada to a greater independence. But there is always this deficiency in our system, namely that of being obliged to go to another country to amend our constitution. I hope, Mr. Speaker, in the course of the present session to have an opportunity to formulate to the house a project which will enable us to amend our own constitution, ourselves, taking good care, however, to preserve the rights of minorities and the spirit of the compact that gave birth to confederation.
If we appreciate the nomination of these
ambassadors, we must, however, deplore the fact that the government has not deemed it advisable to name one to the highest moral power on earth, the Vatican. I state that Canada should hurry to take her place among so many other countries with this international authority, the place on earth where problems are discussed and resolved with the greatest justice and equity. Are we aware of the fact that forty countries are represented at the Vatican? I have here the latest available list, and I think it is well known that those with ambassadors are Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, Peru, Poland. Those with legations are the following: Great Britain, Bolivia, CostaRica, Esthonia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Austria, Hungary, Ireland, Portugal, Roumania,, Santo-Domingo, San Marino, Salvador, Czechoslovakia, Venezuela, Yugoslavia, Malta, Liberia, Lithuania, Monaco, Nicaragua, Panama, Uruguay and Latvia. Everybody knows the President of the United States has his own personal representative. If so many countries find it to their interest to be represented there, wou)d it not be the same for Canada, and would it not be for her one of the best aids in helping her to play the role she is eager to play in the international field?
Therefore I am sure I would be reflecting the opinion of the great majority of the people in this country, Catholics as well as non-Catholics, in urging the government to decide as soon as possible upon the nomina-
5S
The Address-Mr. Dorion

tion of an ambassador to the Holy See. This would surely be the greatest step toward the international status toward which we are heading. Furthermore I should like to tell the Prime Minister, when going to London, that at this imperial conference the finest task he could perform would be to sponsor participation by the Pope in the next peace conference. Since the beginning of the war we have been told we were fighting for democracy and Christian civilization. For us Canadians, we cannot aspire to anything other than the reestablishment of an enduring peace in the world. We cannot expect territorial possessions. We cannot expect much compensation. Therefore, if we wish to reach our end, if we wish to be true to ourselves and to others, we have nothing to do other than to see to it that all the necessary precautions be taken to have this time not twenty years' truce, but a real, everlasting peace. One of the most necessary precautions would most certainly be the attendance at the next peace conference of the most powerful moral authority, the greatest friend of neaee, the greatest advocate of the moral brotherhood of mankind. Moreover, this point of view is shared to-day by all those who really care for the welfare of mankind.
I should like to give as an example a quotation from Time of August 16, 1943. as follows:
"No matter what critics might say, it is scarcely deniable that the church apostolic, through the encyclicals and other papal pronouncements, has been fighting against totalitarianism more knowingly, devoutly and authoritatively, and for a longer time, than any other organized power. Benedict XY was expressly barred from Versailles by a clause in the secret treaty of London. But whether or not the Pope is present, the influence of the Catholic church's peace policy will be tremendous. Most Catholics and non-Catholies alike would agree that a peace that does not embody at least roughly, the papal position on fundamental social issues will bring not social peace but a sword. For when traditional justice fails, retributive justice supervenes.
(Translation.): Mr. Speaker, this opinion of the magazine Time on the participation of the Vatican in the future peace conference is shared by a great many people of all creeds, of all races and of all countries.
It is generally agreed that if peace had been better prepared in 1919, if the peace treaty had not been dictated by the international money powers nor based on the hatred of some prominent figures against certain Catholic countries of Europe; in other words if the peace treaty had been drafted with the cooperation of the greatest moral influence in the world, the Holy See, the world would probably have been saved the horrors of the present conflict.
fMr. Dorion.]
As long as this great international power, the Vatican, is deliberately left aside and excluded from international discussions, the suffering and unhappy peoples of the world will be offered only incomplete and insufficient remedies. The Church is a peacemaker by the very nature of its mission. Suffice it here to recall the many occasions on which the Roman pastors have been successful in putting an end to oppression, in preventing wars, and in securing truces, agreements and peace treaties.
In times gone by, the Pope was requested to act as arbitrator, and history shows that not once had a country any reason to regret having appealed to the Pope for adjusting its differences. One of the first instances where the European nations decided to exclude the Vatican from the discussion of international problems was the Hague convention of 1899. Notwithstanding the express demand of Czar Nicholas II of Russia, notwithstanding the insistence of Queen Wilhelmina, of Holland, notwithstanding the opinions of the experts in international law, the nations decided, on the suggestion of Italy, to exclude the Holy See from the convention. However, less than two years previously, the Seventh World Peace Congress, held in Budapest, under the chairmanship of General Turr, had expressed their gratitude to the Pope for his numerous peace interventions and had humbly and earnestly requested him to remain the champion of the great crusade for the fellowship of all men and to help the civil governments in their efforts toward peaceful mutual understanding.
Neither research congresses, even though independent of all confessional ties, neither the cabinets of reigning sovereigns, although divorced from the Church, could think of an international peace conference from which the Holy See would be excluded.
On August 24, 1898, Count Mouravieff, Minister of Foreign Affairs in Russia, carrying out the instructions of Nicholas II, invited the nations of the world1 to a disarmament conference. This invitation was conveyed to the Vatican on August 30, 1898, by Mr. Tcharykoff, resident minister of the Emperor of Russia appointed to the Holy See.
To this invitation, the Pope replied that he united wholeheartedly with the nations who wished to agree on terms of international peace. On January 16, 1899, the above-mentioned Mr. Tcharykoff sent a second message to the Holy See; it was a circular announcing the programme of the future conference.
Finally, on April 6, 1899, Queen Wilhelmina forwarded the official invitations to the various powers requesting their attendance at the

The Address-Mr. Dorion
meetings that were to take place at The Hague on, May 10 following. These invitations, signed by Monsieur de Baufort, Minister of Foreign Affairs for the Kingdom of the Netherlands, did not, however, reach the Pope, in spite of the wish of Queen Wilhelmina and of Czar Nicholas II.
The reason for this is that, during the first fortnight of February, 1899, Admiral Canevaro, Minister of Foreign Affairs for Italy, informed the Czar and The Hague that unless the Pope were excluded, Italy would not take part in the conference. In spite of the steps taken by the Czar, Italy's objection could not be overruled. A short time before the convention Berlin stepped in, warning the promotors that if one of the great powers kept aloof, Germany would do likewise. As the presence of Germany was absolutely necessary, Italy's pressure was heeded.
During that now famous convention, besides the decisions that were taken, resolutions were drafted for future meetings during which the various nations were to continue the work begun at The Hague. Not content with having succeeded in keeping the Vatican away from the convention itself, Italy objected to the insertion in these resolutions of a clause whose sufficiently general scope might later have opened the door to the Holy See's participation.
Having to face, in connection with the drafting of those resolutions which excluded the Pope, most of the other powers assembled at The Hague, Italy endeavoured to obtain the support of some of the greater nations represented at the convention.
Finally, her objection was endorsed by Great Britain's representative, and once more Italy was successful. However, Queen Wilhelmina, ever anxious to have the Vatican ratify the proceedings and the resolutions of the convention, decided, at the final sitting, to quote the letter which Pope Leo III had sent her in reply to the invitation she had extended to him. That letter expounded principles ' identical to those which Leo XIII had stated some time previously in a eonsistorial address delivered on February 11, 1899.
A few excerpts from that address deserve to be quoted:
Accordingly the church has never been and will never be more concerned about the propagation and the defence of the laws of justice and charity. It is for that purpose that tire church has worked in the whole world and no one can doubt that it has mollified barbaric nations, in imparting to them the love of justice, and that it has thus turned them from the ferocity of warlike customs to lead them to the arts of peace and civilization; to the lowly as well as to the powerful, to those who
obey as well as to those who give commands, it has imposed the obligation of observing justice and refraining from taking up arms for an unjust cause.
And further on:
It applies itself to requesting from God that, for the salvation and prosperity of nations, He should spare them the dangers of war. Accordingly, every time that the need has arisen and the circumstances have permitted, it has no greater concern than to use its authority with a view to restoring harmony and pacifying kingdoms.
The merit of the Hague protocols, those of 1899 and those of 190S, has been to create a remarkable classification of the rules of public international law; there is no doubt that they contain an accurate and able adaptation of the principles of natural law, in accordance with material conditions and the moral standards of modern societies. It is unfortunate that the legal work achieved at the Hague conferences should have remained as unknown and unappreciated as was the case in almost every country of the world and in almost every social circle.
The fundamental principles of the law of nations would have proved, I believe, less inefficient had they been more widely known, more appreciated and endowed with higher moral prestige. The belligerents could not have, without serious moral prejudice to their cause and their country, violated them as universally and as impudently as our enemies did during the last and the present war.
Had a representative of Leo XIII bee* present at the first Hague conference in 1899, and a representative of Piux X at the second in 1907, the decisions and resolutions of those conferences would have gained from the moral prestige that would have bestowed upon them the approval and even the cooperation of the Roman pontiff. In all the countries of the world, the principles of morale and justice arising from these decisions and resolutions would have been impressed upon the conscience of millions by the bishops in their pastoral letters and by the priests from the pulpit.
It is indeed not foolhardy to believe that the cooperation of the representatives of Leo XIII and Pius X at the two conferences of The Hague would have helped to make less ineffective this great work of pacification of peoples.
At the outbreak of the war of 1914-18, the Pope, faithful to his mission of peace, attempted to check what he was perhaps in a better position than anyone else to foresee as a catastrophe from which all peoples would suffer without deriving much benefit. After the conflict had broken out, he endeavoured
The Address-Mr. Dorion

to relieve as much as possible the sufferings of the devastated countries.
The humanitarian works of the Holy See during the last war were innumerable. Its interventions for the exchange of prisoners, for the care of the sick, for the distribution of relief are undeniable and when, in 1918, victory finally crowned the Allied efforts, why was the Pope once more kept away from the discussions which preceded the signing of the peace treaty? Here again the intervention of Italy is seen.
When in 1915 that country agreed to fight on the side of the Allied Nations, a secret treaty was signed between herself, France, Great Britain and Russia. The Italian ambassador in London, Marquess Imperali, upon instructions from his government, conveyed to the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Sir Edward Grey, to the French ambassador, Monsieur Cambon, and to the Russian ambassador, Count Bencken-dorff, a memorandum containing clause 15 w'hich read as follows:
France, Great Britain and Russia shall support Italy's opposition to any proposal tending to introduce a representative of the Holy See in any peace negotiations and in the settlement of matters arising from this war.
This document was signed on the 26th of April, 1915 by the four people I have just mentioned. Therefore, it is not surprising that in 1918 the Pope was not invited to attend the peace conferences of the Allied Nations.
Realizing these facts, is it not true that the instability of the Versailles Treaty appears less amazing? Moreover, why is it that on this page of history, the sacred name of Him from whom proceed all authority, all right and all justice, has not beeil inscribed? It was "in the name of the most Holy Trinity" that in the past the most solemn treaties were signed, those of 1815 as well as the treaties of Utrecht and Westphalia.
Christian institutions were convinced that God alone could put the finishing touch to human agreements to the extent that His spirit penetrated them. What wonderful success resulted from this policy of excluding the sovereign pontiff and of ignoring the rights of Providence 1
The treaty of Versailles has probably lasted for a shorter period of time than any other treaty in history. Is it not very evident that after the present war, when we must start from scratch, it will be absolutely necessary to rectify the mistakes made from 1899 to 1919 and ask the Pope to enlighten by his moral authority the nations which will have the task of drawing up the next peace treaty?
[Mr. Dorion.)
Is there not, at the present time, another secret treaty, another convention designed to keep the Vatican out of international discussions? I hope not, for such a state of things would simply be a repetition of a crime for w'hich we might have to pay very dearly.
It may be said in some circles, even among friends, that it is useless and ill-advised to protest against such an exclusion, for the powers that be have made up their minds to disregard our complaints.
I shall never accept this point of view; a great cause must be defended on the grounds that it is a just cause, and not on the grounds that it pleases everyone.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote a short extract taken from the radio message of His Holiness Pius XII broadcast to the Catholic world on Christmas day 1943:
Give to thirsting humanity a peace that will restore the human race in its own self-esteem and in that of history; a peace on whose cradle will shine not the vengeful glare of hatred and the instinctive unleashed desires of revenge, hut rather the resplendent dawn of a new spirit of universal union; this, strengthened by the supernatural help which is indispensable to the Christian faith, alone can succeed in preserving humanity, after this unfortunate war, from the unspeakable catastrophe of a peace based on false foundations, and consequently no more than an ephemeral illusion.
Monseigneur Deploige, rector of the University of Louvain, speaking at a conference on the Society of Christian nations, said:
To insure peace, in so far as that is possible in this world of ours, recourse to the church of Christ, the great educator of nations, would have been necessary. Indeed, when the task in hand meets so many obstacles the causes of which are buried deep in the human soul, why should the greatest power in the world, heir to the immortal promises of the God of Peace, why should this greatest power alone remain uninvited?
